children.text: The OpenStack deployment uses three Raspberry Pi 5s to host the bootstrap services. MAAS provisions a Dell Inspiron and three Minisforum MS-01s over PXE; the Dell hosts the Juju controller used to build the cloud.
The NAS has an independent lifecycle outside Ceph. That helps protect it from intentional cloud redeployments; it does not substitute for backups or establish recovery time after a failure.

brief.approach: A three-tier bootstrap chain. Three Raspberry Pi 5s, the only machines installed by hand, run MAAS and Landscape on Ubuntu Core with MicroCloud. MAAS provisions a Dell Inspiron, which hosts the Juju controller, and three Minisforum MS-01s over PXE.
brief.outcome: The x86 OpenStack tier can be reprovisioned over PXE. Keeping the NAS outside Ceph separates its lifecycle from cluster redeployments; this is not a measured disaster-recovery or availability result.
brief.problem: I wanted a homelab where I could experiment and break things without worrying about how long it would take to rebuild. Reinstalling an OS across three MS-01s every time got old, and MAAS and Landscape, which manage the machines, need a place to run too.

highlights: Built a three-tier provisioning chain: Raspberry Pi services bootstrap PXE provisioning of the x86 OpenStack nodes.
Separated management and Ceph replication traffic with VLANs; configured link aggregation and jumbo frames for the relevant network paths.
Kept the NAS outside the redeployable cluster so routine cloud rebuilds do not require rebuilding personal storage.
lessons: Most of the failures in this lab have started at Layer 2.
The interesting work is not making the cluster bigger; it is making the existing pieces fit together better and contributing what I learn back to the projects that power it.
